A DOHMH representative stated that after a Request for Proposals is issued, the design process would take approximately 18 to 24 months, followed by a bidding process to select contractors, which would be expected to take approximately nine months. Two ASCPA representatives spoke in support, stating that the organization has been advocating for full-service animal shelters in all five boroughs for close to 20 years. Regarding concerns about the safety of residents and shoppers in the vicinity, they also stated that the Manhattan shelter is in close proximity to a school, several residential buildings, and a hotel, and that complaints about noise, safety, or cleanliness have not been an issue. The ASCPA speakers stated that full-service animal shelters provide vital community resources and do a significant amount of work to deliver social services to animal owners. They stated their belief that the Bronx is considered a “pet desert” that is lacking in pet services. Residents of Co-op City testified in support of the application. They stated that, despite the no-pet policy, many residents own pets, including emotional support and service animals, and other animals that were grandfathered prior to the enactment of the policy that restricts pet ownership. Advocates who spoke in favor of the shelter submitted 4,200 signatures from residents around New York City, and noted that 300 of the signatures were from Co-op City residents, demonstrating that there was support for the shelter within Co-op City. A speaker who identified as a Bronx resident and animal advocate spoke in support of the shelter noting that, in interacting with ACC’s full-service animal shelter in Manhattan, that she had not witnessed animals being dropped off outside of the shelter after hours and was not aware of concerns about cleanliness or noise. On the topic of transportation, the speaker stated that the proposed location is accessible via mass transit. Some Co-op City residents spoke in opposition to the application and stated that 2050 Bartow Avenue could be a potential site for a youth center to serve Co-op City residents. They stated that that a developer had shared a proposal to develop the vacant parcel at 2050 Bartow Avenue as housing with community facility space with the Community Board and Co-op City residents. They noted that the existing community center, located at 3750 Baychester Avenue, does not offer enough space for the broad range of programming the community needs. UNIFORM LAND USE REVIEW The application was certified as complete by the City Planning Commission on September 19, 1983 in accordance with Article 3 of the Uniform Land Use Re- view Procedure (ULURP) and was duly referred to Community Board No. 12. Community Board Public Hearing Community Board No. 12 held a public hearing on the application ( C 830464 ZMX) on October 17, 1983. On October 27, 1983 Community Board No. 12 unanimously recommended by a vote of 14-0 that this request for a zoning change be denied, however, a quorum was not present at the time of the voting. City Planning Commission Public Hearing On November 23, 1983 (Calendar No. 3) the Commission scheduled a public hearing on the proposed change. The hearing was duly held on December 7, 1983 (Calendar No. 26). Four speakers appeared at this time, 3 being in opposition and one, the applicant, in favor of the proposal. An opposing speaker, claiming that his view is shared by some 60 homeowners, stated that there are already too many used car dealers in the neighborhood and that while the proposed change is for the benefit of only one businessman, it will have a negative economic effect on the homeowners in the area. A second resident stated that there are already unsightly car dumps in the area. A third resident stated that the proposed used car lot is to be directly on Palmer Avenue in front-of the residences, rather than on Boston Road itself. In favor of the zoning change, the architect for the owner stated that the portion of the property under consideration will never be developed residentially and that a C-1 zone is not viable. He indicated that the owner would be-willing to buffer the site and locate use(s) in an enclosed building. CONSIDERATION The existing zoning on the subject property and the surrounding area includes a mixture of residential (R4), commercial (C8) and Manufacturing (M1-1). Boston Road, in the area which is the subject of this rezoning request (C 830464 ZMX) is a major thoroughfare developed with a mixture of light manufacturing and commercial uses; no residential development fronts on Boston Road in this area. 2 C 830464 ZMX
